turkey hunting in Macon County.

With the opening of spring turkey season, it always brings back fond memories of hunting trips on my family farm and surrounding property.

As a child, I remember times riding in my father’s old pickup truck across cow pastures and seeing huge flocks of turkeys. At the time I was too young to realize what I was actually witnessing. It was common to see more turkeys than I could count. Those cool crisp blue bird mornings the gobblers would sound off to let the lady hens know that they are the boss of the spring woods.

Back in those days, it was sometimes difficult to decide which gobbler to pursue. There were so many different turkeys gobbling. If you spooked or bumped him off the roost it was no big deal because there were many other gobbling birds to hunt. The male turkeys or gobblers, as I refer to them, would gobble more often throughout the day when I was younger.

What has happened to today’s turkey population and why are they on the decline? I believe that there are many contributing factors.

Let me start by saying that Alabama forest land is not what it used to be. Most of the massive open hardwood bottom land has been harvested for timber production. In many cases, it has re-grown into impenetrable thickets of less desirable trees.

The rolling hillsides that were plentiful with long leaf pine are now nothing short of major pine thickets. The open farm row crop land has grown up with briars and trash trees with little timber value.

Sad but true, none of the above habitats are conducive for wild turkeys.

The only “real” predators back in those days were raccoons and they were hunted nightly, which kept their numbers down. Coyotes were seldom seen or heard. Now coyote numbers are completely out of control. Armadillos or wild hogs were in abundance as they are today.

All of these predators play a major role one way or another in the every day harassment of our state’s wild turkeys.

The Alabama Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Department has kept records on hunter harvest since 1977 and the findings show that the state’s turkey population is on the decrease. In 2007 in Alabama, a mail survey showed the numbers at an all-time high of 73,000 turkeys harvested. This has been on the decline ever since.

The Alabama Wildlife and Freshwater Department is conducting an avid turkey hunter survey this spring.

Friends of Solan

Associated Beneficiary (AB)

In order to support the monastery in the human values that it represents and the global patrimonial management of the project that it leads, the Friends of Solan Association, created in 1995 under the chairmanship of Pierre Rabhi (a french ecologist, founder of the Colibris movement and a founder of the political and scientific movement of agroecology in France) undertakes studies and actions to protect Biodiversity, federating the aspirations and research of today and allowing people with different backgrounds and convictions to participate in Solan’s approach and to promote new approaches of the relationship between man and nature.

The Friends of Solan Association supervises each year trainees whose subject of work and research is the preservation of biodiversity. The interventions focus mainly on the source area of the “Valat de Solan”, a small permanent flow stream with more than 95% of the catchment area located on the site of the Monastery of Solan. The objective of the actions carried out is the maintenance of the flow and the quality of this stream, sheltering Austropotamobius Pallipes, in order to protect this very fragile habitat from a possible drying out.

Since 2009, the Association of Friends of Solan has been responsible of managing the Natura 2000 site FR9102003 “Le Valat de Solan”. The Association also organizes supervised tours of the Solan area in order to testify to the actions taken in favor of biodiversity and to make visitors aware of this patrimonial management of the estate.

It is also crucial that, on steeper slopes and at higher altitudes, forests are purposively managed in such a way as to prevent soil erosion primarily. It is necessary to maintain or strengthen this good practice in the future by applying modern procedures for payments for ecosystem services. We assume that higher locations on the tree line with more than 35% slopes will be the most endangered by erosion processes in the future (in line with [57,59]).
The latest IPCC report [60] mentions the increasing likelihood of pessimistic climate change scenarios. If we estimate that during the short 25-year period after 1990, the warming of 0.83 °C caused an increase in rain erosivity of up to 26%, then in the more pessimistic scenarios of climate development in Slovakia, which anticipates an increase in temperatures in Central Europe by 2–4 °C by the end of the century, rain erosivity can increase by up to 40–80%. At the same time, the potential for mitigating the negative impacts of CC by changing land use is practically exhausted in our case study area. The forest already covers 95% of the catchment area, so the importance of forest management and health care will grow enormously.
For these reasons, it would be highly appropriate for the owners of the Podbrezová Steelworks or water management enterprises to consider contributions from forest owners to support close-to-nature management, which could compensate for increased management costs and reduced income from wood harvests. Harvest restrictions and finer but more expensive forest management should be introduced, particularly near watercourses and spring zones at higher altitudes and on steeper slopes. Ultimately, this can lead to a significant reduction in the cost of maintaining water reservoirs in the long run and, in particular, to improving the quality of the industrial water for fishing or recreation.

Proper unpaved road network maintenance is an extremely important means of reducing soil erosion, sediment yield and siltation [61]. The results showed that, if the volume of sediments from this source could be reduced, the positive effects of vegetation change would be significantly enhanced. The negative effects of climate change on the rate of siltation could not only be offset but even significantly reduced.

Peak Discharge from Catchment of Pine Plantations: Comparison Between Direct Measurement and Empirical Model

Abstrak (Indonesia):
Abstract (English) :

Peak discharge is a crucial component for hydrological cycle. Information on peak discharges is useful for watershed management. Lacking of automatic stream gauge to record the peak discharges encourages a prediction to obtain information on peak discharges. The purpose of the study is to determine the rational runoff coefficient (C) value for pine plantation and to compare the information on peak discharges between a prediction using Rational method with a direct measurement. The study was conducted in Kalipoh catchment covered by pine plantation in Gombong Subdistrict, Kebumen Regency, Central Java Province. Around 95% of the catchment area consists of pine plantation. A prediction of peak discharges using Rational method is multiplication of a constant C, rainfall intensity, and catchment area. The standard value of C for forest area is 0.3. The direct measurement was conducted by installing stream water level recorder using logger. The analysis was conducted for data recorded in 2016. Data analysis showed 37 peak discharge events. The peak discharge of Kalipoh catchment based on direct measurements ranging from 0.02 to 8.34 m /second. Peak discharge prediction using the original formula of Rational method with the C value of 0.3 produced high deviation compared to the peak discharge from direct measurements. The average deviation is 47%. To reduce the deviation, the average rational runoff coefficient (C=0.2) from direct measurements was applied and the result showed the decrease in deviation, in average the deviation was 19.6%.

Keywords: peak discharge, pine, rational method, rational runoff coefficient, rainfall intensity

Media Publikasi :
Proceedings Of IUFRO-INAFOR Joint International Conference 2017
Tyas Mutiara Basuki, Dr., Ir., M.Sc.
